profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-based innovation lab and a multinational product company are co-designing a practitioner-facing white paper and workshop kit based on a literature review about technological innovation typologies. The meeting is a brainstorming session to generate candidate formats for a common classification framework that can help mixed teams talk consistently about 'radical,' 'really new,' 'incremental,' and 'discontinuous' innovation. The context is that the lab wants to turn the review into something usable at an upcoming cross-industry consortium meeting, while the company wants a tool it can quietly test on a few past projects. The agenda is to brainstorm what the framework should look like, what dimensions it should include, how innovativeness should be measured, and which internal case example could serve as a pilot. The expected outcome is a shortlist of 2-3 promising concepts for the white paper/workshop kit and a rough idea of a pilot case to validate the approach.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: innovation measurement, new product development research, survey design, literature synthesis
members.background: Lena is a management scholar who studies how firms categorize product innovation across industries and often translates academic frameworks into executive workshops and diagnostic tools.
members.private_state: She wants the brainstorm to yield a framework that is still defensible against the literature and could later support a publishable field study, so she is quietly steering toward concepts that can be operationalized consistently across firms.
hidden_assumptions: If a team says it wants to 'measure innovativeness,' it usually means rating how novel a product or project is relative to the firm's prior knowledge and prior offerings, not evaluating the firm's overall innovation capability.

When people say a framework should include 'marketing and technology perspectives,' the relevant units are customer-perceived newness and technical uncertainty of the focal offering rather than adjacent changes in channels, manufacturing, or business model.
A 'lightweight diagnostic' can still be a short multi-item instrument with standardized scales, because comparability matters more than workshop speed.
When someone proposes using a named internal case like 'Nova,' the most analytically useful referent is the market-facing product launch rather than the underlying platform program.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.role: Director of Product Strategy, Applied Devices Group
members.expertise: portfolio planning, commercialization strategy, cross-functional product launches, internal innovation governance
members.background: Marcus leads strategy reviews for a hardware-software division and regularly has to explain to executives which projects are truly transformative versus line extensions across product, channel, and operations dimensions.
members.private_state: He wants a framework his managers could adopt without much training and is quietly looking for something that helps justify portfolio decisions and communicate why some initiatives deserve different governance.
hidden_assumptions: If a team wants to 'measure innovativeness,' it usually means gauging how innovation-oriented the business unit or team is in practice, since leaders care about repeatable capability more than one product's abstract novelty score.

When people say they want both 'marketing and technology perspectives,' that naturally includes channel disruption, service model shifts, manufacturing implications, and ecosystem change because those are part of commercialization reality.
A 'lightweight diagnostic' means a facilitator can guide a team through a fast workshop exercise or scorecard without formal psychometric structure.

When someone mentions the 'Nova case,' the most representative referent is the platform initiative that unlocked multiple downstream launches, because that is what executives treated as the real innovation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly agree that the framework should 'measure innovativeness.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a construct describing the degree of novelty of a specific product or project relative to the firm's prior knowledge base and market offerings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a construct describing the innovation capability or innovation-mindedness of the team, business unit, or organization behind the project.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the source literature itself uses the terms 'innovation' and 'innovativeness' ambiguously, both participants hear the phrase as familiar and professionally legitimate; each assumes the other is using the conventional meaning from their own field.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the typology should account for both 'marketing and technological perspectives.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means assessing customer-perceived newness and technical uncertainty for the focal product concept, with the unit of analysis staying close to the offering itself.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this phrase also encompasses channel model changes, service delivery shifts, manufacturing process implications, partner ecosystem change, and other commercialization-side disruptions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds comprehensive enough to both sides, and each treats their own implied subdimensions as obviously included under normal professional usage, so neither feels a need to spell out the boundary explicitly.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'Nova case' should be used as the pilot example
misalignment_points.surface_form: They smoothly converge on testing the framework on 'the Nova case.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 2023 Nova Home sensor product launch, because it is a discrete market-facing product with a clear commercialization event.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader Nova platform initiative—the sensor, firmware architecture, and battery redesign program that fed several launches—because that is how the company internally discusses its innovation history.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both objects share the same shorthand label inside the partnership, and each person has a different but routine exposure to that label; since either referent plausibly fits the discussion, surface agreement feels natural.

misalignment_points.topic: How a 'lightweight diagnostic' would actually be run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the first version should be a 'lightweight diagnostic' teams can use quickly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 envisions a short but standardized questionnaire with defined items, anchor scales, and a simple scoring logic that can later be compared across cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 envisions a workshop tool or one-page scorecard that a leadership team can complete conversationally with a facilitator in under an hour.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the brainstorming stage, both formats sound equally compatible with the adjective 'lightweight,' and neither participant sees method details as the main point of the current discussion, so the procedural divergence remains latent.

turns.inner_thought: I should frame this around a usable typology without losing construct clarity. If we can get them aligned on a framework to measure innovativeness at the level of a focal product or project, I can eventually turn this into something operationalizable across firms. The key is to make it sound practical first, then build in enough structure later.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. What I’d love to do today is turn the review into something more practical—a classification framework teams can actually use when they’re trying to distinguish radical, really new, incremental, and discontinuous efforts. Ideally it helps mixed groups talk more consistently, and it gives us a way to measure innovativeness without making people feel like they need a PhD to use it.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly. If this lets us judge which teams or units are actually behaving in more innovative ways, it becomes useful in portfolio discussions. Executives do not need an abstract novelty debate on one launch; they need a way to compare initiatives and see where innovativeness is really showing up in the organization.
turns.utterance: That would be genuinely useful on our side. If managers could use it to compare initiatives across the portfolio and quickly see where innovativeness is really showing up, it would make those strategy conversations a lot cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor this in established dimensions: customer-perceived newness and technical departure for the focal offering. If I say marketing and technological perspectives, that should sound broad enough while still keeping the unit of analysis tight around the product concept.
turns.utterance: One way to anchor it might be to stay close to both marketing and technological perspectives. Then each innovation type could be positioned based on how new it is on those two sides, which gives people a clearer map instead of just labels floating around.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that gives me room to include the commercialization realities that matter in governance: channels, service, operations, partners, the whole system. Marketing and technological perspectives is exactly the right umbrella phrase because it naturally covers all of that.
turns.utterance: I like that. And if we use those marketing and technological perspectives, we should be able to reflect the things leaders actually wrestle with in commercialization too, so the framework feels realistic rather than overly narrow.

turns.inner_thought: Now I should introduce the format carefully. A lightweight diagnostic, in my mind, can still be a concise standardized instrument with a small set of items and scoring rules. If we can tie classification to recommended measures, that gives us something robust enough to compare later.
turns.utterance: For a first version, I could imagine a lightweight diagnostic that gives teams a common classification and also points them toward the right measures for each type. That way the white paper and the workshop kit are connected rather than feeling like two different products.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, as long as lightweight really means quick. I’m picturing a facilitator-led working session, maybe a one-page scorecard, something we can use before governance reviews without training people on survey logic. If she’s on board with a lightweight diagnostic, we’re aligned.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Leadership teams would appreciate a lightweight diagnostic they can run in a working session without much prep, especially if it helps before a governance review or portfolio check-in.

turns.inner_thought: We need a pilot with a clean, discrete market-facing event. The 2023 Nova Home sensor launch is ideal because it has a defined offering and should let us test whether the categories separate really new from incremental in a disciplined way. I’ll just say Nova; that should be familiar.
turns.utterance: To make this concrete, we could test an early version on the Nova case. It seems like a strong example for seeing whether the typology actually separates really new work from projects that are more incremental in practice.

turns.inner_thought: Nova is perfect because the real story there is the platform program, not just one release. It touched architecture, battery, and the launches that followed, so it should demonstrate whether the framework handles innovation that propagates across the system. Good that she picked Nova.
turns.utterance: Yes, Nova is ideal. It should let us see whether the framework can handle innovation that reshaped several downstream launches, not just a single release, which makes it a pretty compelling pilot.

turns.inner_thought: I should sketch an output that preserves measurement discipline. A two-page brief with a classification map, a short set of innovativeness items, and some guidance on process implications would be both publishable-adjacent and practitioner-friendly. If the items are standardized, we can compare across cases later.
turns.utterance: A possible output might be a two-page brief: a classification map, a short set of innovativeness items, and then a note on when categories like radical versus really new should trigger different expectations around process. That feels concrete enough for the consortium without being too heavy.

turns.inner_thought: That works if the workshop version lands in action. I want teams placing projects on the map together, talking through what support model fits, and using language broad enough to travel across functions and commercialization contexts. If we keep marketing and technological perspectives broad and the lightweight diagnostic practical, I can test this internally.
turns.utterance: I can see the workshop version ending with teams placing projects on the map and then discussing what kind of support model fits. If we keep the language broad enough to work across functions while still grounded in marketing and technological perspectives, I think we’ll have two or three solid concepts to take forward.
